about: The words of the chain saga_danes_norway, THE KINGS' SUMMER, 812 to 815 (cards: Data/encounters/chain_saga_danes_norway_793.json; page: Design/content/chains/saga_danes_norway.md). Keys are chain_saga_danes_norway.<card>.<what>; out_* are the outcome texts named in each option's note; art.<card id> says what the card's picture shows. Nothing is quoted from any translation: the annals' facts are told in our own words. Harald, Reginfrid, Anulo, Hemming, Sigfred, Osfrid of Skane and Godfred's sons are real; Eskil, Styr and Asny are invented. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: The count of the dead
The landing is short of men. At the alehouse a young man with a new arm ring is buying for two kings nobody had heard of a year ago, and the ale-wife is counting on her fingers who has not come home.
Hemming died in his bed in the winter, which no king here has done for a while. Then Sigfred and Anulo fought over the seat. Both are dead. So is everyone who stood near them.
You were not here last year. Hemming died, and Sigfred and Anulo fought over the seat, and both fell. We have had a year to count since. The count has not got smaller.
The Franks will have a number for it by now. They like a number. I have nineteen names, and that is only the men who drank here.
Eleven from this bank of the river. I brew less. Nobody has thanked me for the saving.
Anulo's side held the field, so Anulo's brothers are kings. Harald and Reginfrid. Two, so that there is one to spare. I am Eskil, and I buy for them.
A king who gives no feast is not king for long. I will take what you have. Some silver now, and the rest on a split stick, to be made good at the hall at Hleidr.
You have come to a king-making with an empty boat. That is a Frisian thing to do. Come again with wine, and come soon.
Sell to the new kings: part in silver now, the rest on a split stick
Buy the ale-wife a cup and ask where the beaten men went
Say kings are no Frisian's business, and ask what wine fetches

Eskil weighs out thirty pennies' weight of cut silver and notches a hazel stick for the rest. He splits it down the middle and gives you the half with the bark on. It is good at the hall at Hleidr, he says, for as long as his kings are. He says it as a joke.

She drinks the cup first. The beaten men swore to the new kings, she says, because the other thing to do was to be dead. Some swore and then went east, by Skane and over the water to the Svear. Godfred's sons are there. They were boys when their father was killed. They are not boys now.

Eskil laughs and tells you. Two new kings are feasting every lord who might otherwise remember he fought against them, and wine is a third dearer than it was at midsummer. He seems to think you have said something wise.
A stick in Skane

On the old market ground at the river mouth a man with a bound arm is waiting for a boat east. He has a rune stick he wants carried the other way, to Sliesthorp, and the farmer Hebbi is the only one here who can read it.
I am Styr. I stood with Sigfred, and then I swore to the two brothers with Sigfred's blood still on my shoes. I find the oath sits badly. I am going where Godfred's sons are.
This stick goes to Asulf, who sells people at Sliesthorp and knows every lord in Jutland by what he owes. It asks one thing. He will pay you when he has read it.
Osfrid of Skane swore on the Eider with the great men two summers back. Since then he has been careful to be on nobody's side that anybody can name. He will die old.
My father said: two kings on one bench, and the bench gets no warmer. He said it about his brothers, but it will do.
Carry the stick to the dealer Asulf at Sliesthorp
Have Hebbi read it aloud, and leave it where it lies
Say you carry cloth, not sticks, and ask Hebbi about amber

Styr gives you twenty pennies' weight from a purse that has not much more in it. Hebbi reads the stick to you before it goes in your chest, since a man should know what he carries. It asks who in Jutland will rise when the kings are away from home. It does not say when that will be. Styr says kings are always away from home sooner or later.

Hebbi reads it with his thumb, slowly, and shows you which stave is which. It asks who in Jutland will rise when the kings are away from home. You hand it back. Styr looks at you for a while and then shrugs with his good shoulder. Another boat will take it, he says, or none will, and Godfred's sons will come home either way.

Styr puts the stick back in his shirt. Hebbi is pleased to talk about something else. There was an easterly four nights ago and the shore below the dunes is yellow with amber. Every child in the river mouth has a bag of it, and the price has dropped by a fifth.
Two on the high seat

The hall at Hleidr is feasting two kings on one high seat. Half the benches are filled with men who fought against them a year ago. The steward wants rope for a fleet, and says where the fleet is going.
I have seated men tonight beside the men who killed their brothers. It took me four days. Nobody has thanked me, which means I did it well.

When the barley is in the ground the kings go north to the Vik. The chiefs there keep the landing gifts and send none south. The fleet wants rope. Eight coils of the good kind, before the ships go down the fjord.
You have a split stick of Eskil's. I have the other half. I had hoped you were dead, but I see you are not, so we shall weigh.
Two kings. I have had to make every verse twice, once for each, and of the same length. Reginfrid counts the lines. Harald does not, which is worse.
You have the face of a man who has been in Skane. So has half this bench. Nobody here says so aloud. I would not either.
Take the fleet's order for rope
Lay your half of the split stick on the trestle
Sit low on the bench and listen to the skald

Asgaut names the weight once. Eight coils of rope at well over what the strand pays, to be on the landing before the ships go down the fjord. He does not ask whether you can find it. Across the fire the two kings are sharing one horn, and each is watching how much the other drinks.

The halves fit. Asgaut weighs out a hundred and forty pennies' weight in cut rings and does not round it either way. While he weighs, Thorulf says the old lay of this hall, the one about a king who paid his men in gold. He says it loudly, and in the direction of the high seat.

You sit by the door with the grooms. Thorulf comes down the hall with a riddle about a beast with eight horns and no head, which many follow, and leaves it with you. He looks at the high seat while he says it. From the grooms you learn more than from the benches: the ships go north when the barley is sown, and both kings go with them. Nobody stays behind to keep the hall but the steward.
A boat nobody looks at twice

The chief has walked down from the hall himself. Word has come up the coast that the kings of the Danes are gathering ships. He looks at your boat for some time, as a man looks at a horse he does not mean to praise.
The Danes have two kings this year. They are coming to ask me a question, with a host, so that I shall hear it clearly. I would like to give one answer to both. I am told that is the difficulty.
Your boat is not handsome. Could it carry my daughter and one chest round to the Karmsund, to the woman who keeps the keys on the ness? Nobody counts what is in a boat like that.
The chest is heavier than I am. Father says that if we meet a ship, I am your sister's girl and it is full of whetstones. Some of it is.
You have sat in their hall this winter. Tell me what they want, and say it plainly. I am an old man and courtesy takes me a long time.
Take the girl and the chest round to the Karmsund
Tell him what was said in the hall at Hleidr: they want the landing gifts, not his head
Say four men and a load of cloth are no guard for a chief's daughter

The chest comes down at dusk on a sledge, under hides. Asny sits on it. Asgrim pays forty pennies' weight for the passage and says the rest will be owed, which from him is a large word. He does not wave. He stands on the jetty until the first skerry hides you.

You tell him what the steward said: the landing gifts, sent south each year, and an oath. Nobody at Hleidr spoke of his hall or his head. Asgrim hears it out and asks three more questions to be sure. Then he has four good hones brought down for you. A man can give away gifts, he says. It is the giving of them that he minds.

He nods, as if you had told him the wind. It is a fair answer, he says, and he would have thought less of the boat if you had said yes at once. He will find another way. The hones are stacked on the strand unsold. Nobody wants to buy stone in a summer when iron is coming.
The woman with the keys

The girl and the chest go up the path to the hall on the ness. On the strand a ship's chief is fitting out for the summer, and he would like to know where the kings of the Danes have taken their ships.
Asgrim's chest. I shall weigh it before your eyes and again before his, and it will weigh the same. Tell him Gunnhild said so.
The girl can stay until her father has found his answer. She will learn to brew. Everybody who stays here learns to brew.
A Frisian from the Vik. You will have seen ships. I hear the Danes have two kings and that both have gone the same way. Which way was that?
The sound is narrow and the stream runs like a mill race. There are five stones on the far shore that lean toward it. Stay three days and I will give you every mark in a verse you cannot lose.
Hand over the girl, take what is owed, and know nothing about kings
Tell the ship's chief the Danish host is in the Vik, and every coast south of it unwatched
Stay three days for the skald, and learn the sound from him

Gunnhild weighs the chest, then weighs out sixty pennies' weight for you from her own purse, to be settled with Asgrim later. You tell the ship's chief that you saw fog and a great many gulls. He laughs and says a Frisian sees what he is paid to see. He goes back to his rigging.

You tell him. Both kings and every ship they have are in the Vik until harvest, and there is nobody at home on the coasts to the south. He cuts a piece from his arm ring and does not weigh it. Four ships go down the sound within the week. In autumn, word comes that Northmen have been in Frisia and carried off men and women. You know some of the place names.

Three days. Hallgrim walks you along the sound and gives you each mark in a line of verse: the five leaning stones, the green mound, the skerry that shows at half ebb. He makes you say it back until he stops wincing. Gunnhild weighs the chest and pays what is owed. The girl waves from the brew-house door.
The host in the fjord

The fjord is full of Danish ships drawn up stem by stem. The market is shut and the cattle are gone inland. A host eats, and the kings' man is paying twice the market for anything that can be eaten or can carry.
The Frisian. I buy in the south and you are there, I buy in the north and you are there. Either you follow kings about or kings follow you.
The chiefs here have hidden their cattle and found their manners. We have a great many men and nothing to roast. Bread, ale, a hull to carry fodder. I pay double, in silver, today.
Tomorrow on the heath I swear on the ring to two kings by name. I have asked whether one oath will do for both. It will. I had not hoped for so much thrift from Danes.
They have counted my cattle and my benches. They have found me poorer than they were told. I am obliged to your boat for that.
It is as you said. The gifts and an oath. I have kept my head, and I use it now mostly for nodding.
Sell the host bread, ale and carriage at the kings' price
Go up to the thing heath and stand witness when the chief swears
Tell the kings' man what is said in Skane: Godfred's sons are coming home

For nine days your boat carries fodder and ale between the farms and the ships. Eskil pays as he said, a hundred and eighty pennies' weight, and counts it out where the whole strand can see. The people of the market watch from their doors. Nobody says anything. They do not need to.

On the heath the chiefs of the Vik lay a hand on the ring, one after another, and swear to Harald and to Reginfrid by name. The lawman asks who of the strangers saw it. You say that you did. It costs you a day of trade. Asgrim says nothing to you on the way down, and has ale sent to the boat.

Eskil hears you to the end without smiling, which is new. Then he goes up the strand to the kings' tent and is in it a long time. He comes back with a ring for you, sixty pennies' weight. The kings will take the oaths and go home at once, he says, not after harvest. He does not say they believed it. He says they would rather be laughed at in their own hall than out of it.

Eskil hears you out and laughs. Boys among the Svear, he says, and a few sore losers. The kings have the whole host of the Danes in this fjord, and it has taken them a year to gather it. They will go home after harvest, when the Vik has paid. He advises you to stick to cloth.
The brother given back

Sixteen lords of the Danes have ridden home from swearing peace with the Franks, and they have brought the kings' brother with them. He has Frankish shoes and nobody to give his news to: both kings are in the north.
I am Hemming. My brothers asked the emperor for me two summers running and went north the week I came. I am told it is a great honour to be asked for.
You are a Frisian, so you have been everywhere and will say you saw nothing. I have been so long among the Franks that I know that answer. What is said in the harbours? I ask as a brother.
Sixteen of ours and as many of theirs, beyond the Elbe. They swore, and nobody was sold. A poor summer for my trade. The border is open, though, and that is good for yours.
I hear you have something of mine from Skane. A stick. I do not read sticks in the street. Come behind the pen.
Give Asulf the stick from Skane
Tell Hemming what Skane says, and that his brothers should come home
Sell to the lords' following and say nothing to anyone

Asulf reads the stick with his lips moving. Then he puts it in the fire and weighs out a hundred pennies' weight from his arm ring, and adds two marten skins without being asked. He does not say what answer he will send. He says that he has always bought from whoever won, and that it is useful to know a little early who that will be.

You tell him. Godfred's sons are among the Svear with every man who lost last year, and they are waiting for the kings to be away from home. Hemming goes quite still. Then he asks which is the fastest ship in the harbour and who owns it. By evening it is gone down the Slie with his own man aboard. He gives you forty pennies' weight and two cups of Frankish glass, which are all he has that is his.

The sixteen have followings, and the followings have been three weeks on Saxon bread. You sell what you have for twenty-five pennies' weight above the strand price. The talk at the booths is all of one thing: peace is sworn, and a man may cross the Eider with goods again.

At Sliesthorp they say sixteen lords of the Danes have sworn peace with the emperor's men beyond the Elbe, and that the kings' brother Hemming has been given back. The kings were not there. They are in the Vik with the host.
Leaf fall
The sons of Godfred are home from the Svear with every man who lost last year, and the country has to choose again. Two men are waiting at your boat. They are not waiting together.
Godfred's sons are home. The kings came back from the north with a tired host and found the country had got up before them. There was one fight. It was not a long one.
We are out. I will not dress it. Harald and Reginfrid have two ships and the men who will not leave them. That is still more than Godfred's sons had last year.

We were home before the leaf fell, with the host whole. Godfred's sons landed to find the benches full. They have not had their easy fight. They have not gone away either. It will be settled in spring.
Somebody told the kings. We know it was somebody. I am going back over the water tonight, and I am looking at every boat in this harbour before I go.
A king does not forget who stood by him when he was worth nothing. Kings say so, at least. Give me your hand on it now, and we shall both find out.
The sons of a king who made this market do not ask who a merchant sold to last year. They ask who he sells to now. They will want wine. Their father always did.
You are the man with the stick from Skane. Asulf told us. Come to Sliesthorp when the roads are dry. You will not need to wait at the gate.
Give Eskil your hand: the house stands by Harald, whatever comes of him
Sell to the men who have won, and ask to be shown to Godfred's sons
Tell both that a Frisian has no king here, and go north in spring

You give Eskil your hand. He holds it a moment longer than the custom is. The kings will try again when the roads are dry, he says. If it goes well, come to the hall at Hleidr. If it goes badly, be at Ripa after the spring sowing, with your boat and what you know about the flats. The other man has already walked away.

The envoy buys what you have, sixty pennies' weight above the strand, and pays it from a purse of Svear make. Come to Sliesthorp when the roads are dry, he says, and ask for the youngest. The older ones do not talk to merchants yet. Eskil watches the silver change hands. He does not say anything, and you find you remember it.

You tell them both that your house has a count at Dorestat and finds one lord enough. Each of them thinks it is a poor answer and neither can fault it. In the Vik there is an oath sworn last summer to kings who have other things to think about, and a market that has seen no southern keel since. You will go north when the ice is off the fjords.
A king over the flats

Two ships lie in the river below Ripa with half their oars unmanned. Reginfrid is dead. His brother means to reach the emperor's shore before Godfred's sons reach him, and no Dane aboard knows the channels behind the islands as a Frisian does.
We tried again when the roads were dry. Reginfrid is dead. So is the eldest of Godfred's sons, which is fair. But they had brothers to spare and we did not.
The old emperor is dead as well, since winter. His son is the man to reach now. By sea outside the islands they will have us. Inside, over the flats, we need someone who knows which water is water.
I have been a king for two years and I have been at home for one of them. Take me south, Frisian. I will pay you now, or I will pay you better when I come back. I mean to come back.
You still carry our split stick. The other half is at Hleidr, in a hall we do not hold. The king has two ships and men for one. Think about that before you name your price.
Lead his ships through the channels to the Frisian shore, for a king's thanks
Lead him over and ask nothing now: take his ring as a token for the day he comes home
Lead him over, and take the second ship he cannot man in place of silver

Three tides, lying dry on the sand between them, with your boat ahead and a man sounding with a pole. On the third evening the king of the Danes wades ashore in the emperor's land with forty men. He breaks two gold-washed rings and a silver one for you, eight hundred pennies' weight, and says before all of them that your house is under his hand. It is a small hand this year. He goes inland to find the emperor, and you hear later that he found him.

You lead him over in three tides and take what a careful man would take for the pilotage, no more: four hundred pennies' weight, and six casks of wine he has no use for where he is going. He asks what else. You say he may pay the rest when he is king at home. Harald looks at you for a long time. Then he takes the ring from his own arm, the one with the two beast heads, and puts it in your hand. Show that, he says, to me or to any man of mine, in any year.

You lead him over in three tides. On the Frisian shore Eskil has the second ship stripped of its shields and handed to you where it lies, with its mast, its oars and a hundred and fifty pennies' weight to close the count. She is a sound Danish hull, oak below and built to carry. Harald does not come to see it done. A king minds losing a ship more than a kingdom, Eskil says, because the ship he chose himself.
One on the high seat

There is one king on the high seat at Hleidr and an empty place beside him with a sword laid on it. Godfred's sons are back over the water. The king has sent down the hall for the Frisian who said the right thing in the right summer.
They met when the roads were dry. Reginfrid fell, and Godfred's eldest fell, and after that the sons had no stomach for it. They are among the Svear again. It is a long way to come twice.
I need make each verse only once now. I find I miss the work. Do not tell him.
We were told to come home, and we came home, and I am here. My brother is not. I do not thank you for the half of it. For the other half, ask.
There is a story on the benches that you carried a stick for the other side too. The king has heard it. He has decided it is a story. I should ask for something modest.
Ask a seat in the hall for your house, and take the king's gift
Ask nothing for yourself: ask the king's peace for every Frisian keel at his markets
Ask a plot inside the wall at Sliesthorp, and say the hall is too far from the sea

The steward shows you a place on the bench, not high and not by the door, and says it is yours and your son's whenever the hall is feasting. The king sends down rings to the weight of nine hundred pennies. Thorulf puts a Frisian in a verse for the first time, and rhymes him with a kind of gull. Over the water, Godfred's sons have also learned the name of your house.

The hall goes quiet, because a man who asks nothing for himself is either a fool or dangerous. Harald decides you are neither. It is said before the benches: a Frisian keel lies at the king's markets on the Slie and at Ripa under the king's peace, and pays the king nothing at the gate. He adds six hundred pennies' weight and six marten skins so that nobody can say he was given advice for nothing. The Danes on the benches look at you differently. So, when they hear of it, will Godfred's sons.

The king laughs for the first time since spring. A merchant, he says, to the bone. You are given a plot inside the wall at Sliesthorp, twelve paces of shore with a lane behind it, and seven hundred pennies' weight to build on it. The Wends from Reric are your neighbours on one side. On the other is a man who was for Godfred's sons until last autumn and would rather you did not mention it.
Godfred's sons

Godfred's sons hold the kingdom, one fewer than they were in spring. The youngest of them is at the gate in the wall his father built, learning who trades here. He has been four years among the Svear and counts everything twice.
My father built this wall and brought these merchants here in his ships. He did not ask them. I have been asking people things all morning. It is slower. I am told it lasts longer.
My eldest brother is dead, and so is Reginfrid. Harald has run to the Franks. He will be back with somebody else's army. Men like him always are. Until then there are markets to keep.
I was carried here from Reric in his father's ship, with my scales in my lap. I have done well out of it. I would still not call it an invitation. The young one listens, which the old one did not.
Asulf says the stick from Skane came in your boat. We counted the men who rose for us by what was written back. So I count you with them.
You sold bread to their host in the Vik. So did everyone with bread. I notice it, and I set it down, and that is all I do with it this year.
Ask a plot inside the wall, and sell the new kings what a king-making needs
Remind him who carried the stick, and ask for the Wend Dragomir as your man here
Ask only that your boat pass the gate as it did under his father

Four kings at once need four times the wine, and nobody in the harbour has more of it than you do. By the end of the week you have eight hundred pennies' weight and a plot inside the wall, paced out by Horik himself, who paces it twice. He tells you what the ground rent is before you ask. He is the first lord you have met who knew.

Horik sends for Dragomir and says it before the gate: the Wend keeps this Frisian's goods and sells them in his name, and whoever robs the one robs the king's guest. Dragomir bows to exactly the depth the thing is worth. From the kings' store come eight marten skins and six sacks of amber, and seven hundred pennies' weight for the wine. Among the Danes it is now known that your house was for Godfred's sons before it was safe to be.

It is a small thing to ask, and Horik distrusts it for a moment for that reason. Then he has it said at the gate: this boat passes as it did in Godfred's day and pays the king nothing on what it sells. You make six hundred pennies' weight in the week of the king-making, and keep all of it. Dragomir says you asked for too little. He says it as a compliment.
Two kings for one answer

The market at Skiringssal has had no wine, salt or glass for a year and a half, and the strand is stacked with hones nobody came for. On the heath the chiefs of the Vik are asking what an oath is worth when the men it was sworn to have lost their kingdom.
I swore to two kings in the summer. By winter they had no kingdom. I tell it without smiling. It costs me some effort.
They went home early, and they kept their kingdom, and so I am their man. Somebody gave them good advice. I hope he was paid for it, since I was not.
An oath is sworn to a man, at a place, before witnesses. If the man is gone, the place remains and the witnesses remain. The thing must say which of the three the oath belongs to.
My daughter has been a year on the Karmsund. I am told she brews. I should like to see that, and the chest, in that order.
You fed them when they lay in my fjord. It was good silver, I am sure. Thordis at the alehouse has kept the count of it for you, in case you forgot.
Tell him his daughter and his chest are safe on the Karmsund, and offer to fetch them
Go up to the heath and say before the thing what you saw sworn, and to whom
Leave the heath to the chiefs, and be the first cargo into a hungry market

You fetch them before midsummer. The chest weighs what Gunnhild said it would. Asgrim seats you above his steward and tells the hall how he sent his daughter round the coast in a boat nobody looked at twice. In his telling the plan is his. He gives you ten of the best hones and seven hundred pennies' weight, and says your house lands on his shore without a gift from now on. Then he asks whether you have a son, and how old, and whether the boy would not do well with a few winters in the Vik.

You say it before the thing, in their tongue, slowly: the chiefs laid a hand on the ring and swore to Harald and to Reginfrid, by name, and to no one else and to no kingdom. The lawman asks you twice. Then he says the law: an oath to a man does not pass to the man who drove him out. The Vik keeps its own landing gifts. The chiefs give you nine hundred pennies' weight between them and six good pots of soapstone, and Asgrim says that a Frisian has cost the Danes more with one sentence than he ever did with his cattle.

The first southern keel in a year and a half. Wine goes at half as much again as you have ever had for it, and hones can be had for the carrying. You clear six hundred and fifty pennies' weight in four days. The women of the market settle among themselves that the Frisian should have a booth of his own, so that he comes back. Asgrim lets them think they decided it.
Over the Eider

A host of Saxons and Wends has crossed the Eider with Harald among them and is burning its way north. Godfred's sons have taken two hundred ships to an island and are watching from there. The ferryman has had a busy week.

Seven days' march to the shore, and there they sit. Godfred's sons sit on an island a short row off, with two hundred ships. Neither will cross the water to the other. I have seen cows settle a field with more blood.
Your king is with them. The one you took over the flats. He has come home with somebody else's army, and it is burning his own farms for him.
Your friends are on the island. A king on an island is still a king. Their father would have gone out and fought. Their father is dead.
It will end with hostages. It always does. Somebody's sons will go south to learn to wear shoes, and everyone will call it peace.
Carry bread and ale south to the host, where Harald will know your sail
Carry the country people and their goods over the Slie, at the ferryman's rate
Lie behind the wall and watch what kind of war it is

Harald knows your sail and has his men pay first and ask afterwards: a hundred and fifty pennies' weight for bread and ale, in Saxon silver. He looks older. He asks whether the hall at Hleidr still leans. The host stays three days on the shore, takes forty hostages from the country round about and goes home over the Eider. Harald goes with it.

For six days you carry farm people over the Slie with their kettles, their geese and their grandmothers, at the ferryman's rate and no higher. It comes to forty pennies' weight. Hallbjorn says it is the first time he has seen a Frisian leave silver on a strand. Then the host turns south with forty hostages, and the same people want carrying back.

You lie behind Godfred's wall with the Wends from Reric, who have seen a town burned and are calm about it. The host never comes so far. It wastes the farms to the south, takes forty hostages and goes home. For a month afterwards hides are cheap: the cattle that could not be hidden were killed, by their owners or by the Saxons.

At Sliesthorp they say the emperor's Saxons and the Wends crossed the Eider to put Harald back, and that Godfred's sons lay on an island with two hundred ships and would not fight. The host took forty hostages and went home. Harald went with it.

A grey spring morning on a Danish landing with too few men on it: in the door of an alehouse a woman counts on her fingers, and beside her a young man with a bright new arm ring holds a hazel stick split down the middle; behind them, boats drawn up with nobody working on them.

A sandy river mouth in Skane under a wide sky, cattle grazing on old house plots: a man with his arm bound in a sling holds out a short rune-cut stick, and a heavy-shouldered farmer with a sack of antler on his back bends to read it with his thumb.

The inside of a great timber hall at night, seen from the low benches by the door: a long fire down the middle, and beyond it two kings on one high seat sharing a horn; in front, a tall stooped steward with an iron key at his belt and a slight red-bearded poet in a blue cloak.

Dusk on a new timber jetty in the Vik, skerries beyond: a tall spare chief in a red cloak with two grey hounds looks down into a small Frisian boat; beside him a girl of fifteen sits on an iron-bound chest on a sledge, half covered with hides.

A narrow sound with a fast stream under a bright windy sky, a hall on the ness above and great mounds on the skyline: a woman with keys at her belt weighs a chest on a beam scale on the strand, a girl beside her; behind, a big man rigs a longship and looks over his shoulder.

A summer noon in a fjord crowded with Danish warships drawn up stem by stem, shields along the rails and cooking smoke everywhere: the market booths on the shore stand shuttered, and on the empty strand a kings' man counts out silver in plain sight.

Late afternoon inside the earth wall at Sliesthorp: a man in Frankish shoes and a short Frankish cloak stands alone among dusty horsemen dismounting; at the side a stout dealer with a plaited beard and a hazel switch watches from beside a wattle pen.

An autumn evening on a landing with yellow leaves on the water: a small boat at the jetty, and two men waiting at either end of it with their backs to each other, one with a worn kings' arm ring, one with a sword of Svear make; beyond the roofs, the masts of many newly come ships.

Low tide on the flats of the Wadden Sea at dawn, water and sand the same colour: a small Frisian boat ahead with a man sounding with a pole, and behind it two Danish ships with half their oars shipped; in the stern of the first, a man in a red cloak looks back at the shore.

The great hall at Hleidr by firelight: one king on a high seat made for two, and on the empty half a sword laid crosswise; a Frisian merchant stands before him in the middle of the floor, with every face on the benches turned his way.

A bright morning at the gate in the earth wall at Sliesthorp: a young man of nineteen in a king's red cloak too new for him paces out a plot of shore with long steps; a grey Wendish merchant with a scale case watches, and the harbour beyond is full of ships with shields still on them.

A flat heath above the Vik under a high spring sky: a ring of chiefs standing round a lawman who holds a silver oath ring, a Frisian stranger among them; far below, the market strand piled with unsold whetstones and one small boat at the jetty.

Midsummer on the Slie under a sky smudged with far smoke to the south: an old barefoot ferryman with a white tail of hair poles a flat boat loaded with farm people, geese and kettles; behind them, the earth wall of Sliesthorp with men standing on it.
